lessons.title: Liquidity Ratios: Current Ratio, Quick Ratio and Their Limits

children.text: A credit officer opens your balance sheet and looks at two numbers before anything else. A supplier deciding whether to give you 60 days of credit looks at the same two. They are the current ratio and the quick ratio, and between them they take about fifteen seconds to compute.

That speed is the attraction and also the danger. This lesson shows you how to compute all three liquidity ratios properly, what the Indian benchmarks actually are and where they came from, and the four situations where these ratios will mislead you badly.
The Three Ratios, Computed on a Real Balance Sheet

We continue with Sunrise Ceramics Ltd from Chapter 1: current assets of ₹122 crore, current liabilities of ₹101 crore, inventories of ₹42 crore and prepaid expenses of ₹1.5 crore inside other current assets.

body.caption: Can short-term assets cover short-term dues at all?
Can they cover the dues without having to sell a single tile?
What if nothing gets collected and nothing gets sold?

children.text: The
current ratio
of 1.21 says the business has ₹1.21 of current assets for every rupee due within the year. The
quick ratio
of 0.78 says that once you set aside the tiles in the warehouse, it can cover only 78 paise of every rupee. The
cash ratio
of 0.06 says the actual cash on hand covers 6 paise of it.

markDefs.definition: Current assets divided by current liabilities. A rough measure of whether short-term resources cover short-term obligations.
Current assets excluding inventory and prepaid expenses, divided by current liabilities. Also called the acid test ratio.
Cash and cash equivalents divided by current liabilities. The strictest liquidity test, ignoring everything that still has to be sold or collected.

stats.label: Current ratio
stats.context: Below the 1.33 benchmark Indian bankers still carry in their heads

stats.label: Quick ratio
stats.context: Below 1, so the company depends on selling inventory to meet its dues

stats.label: Cash ratio
stats.context: Normal for a manufacturer, which holds working assets rather than cash

body.text: Read the three together, not separately. A wide gap between the current ratio and the quick ratio always means the same thing: this business carries a lot of inventory. Whether that is a problem depends on whether the inventory moves, which no ratio here can tell you.

body.title: Compute the quick ratio
body.prompt: Deccan Polymers reports inventories of ₹26 crore, trade receivables of ₹34 crore, cash of ₹3 crore, other current assets of ₹5 crore and total current liabilities of ₹50 crore. Ignoring prepaid expenses, what is its quick ratio? Give your answer to two decimal places.
body.explanation: Quick assets are ₹68 crore of current assets minus ₹26 crore of inventory, which is ₹42 crore. Divided by ₹50 crore of current liabilities, that is 0.84. Its current ratio of 1.36 looks healthier, and the gap between the two is the inventory.

children.text: Where the 1.33 Benchmark Comes From
Ask an Indian banker for the minimum acceptable current ratio and you will hear 1.33 almost every time. That number is not an accounting rule or a regulation. It is the residue of a 1975 committee.

The Tandon Committee, set up by the Reserve Bank of India to bring discipline to bank working capital lending, recommended that borrowers fund a meaningful share of their current assets from their own long-term sources. Under its second method of lending, the borrower contributes 25% of total current assets and the bank funds the rest, which arithmetically produces a current ratio of about 1.33. The Chore Committee in 1979 pushed larger borrowers towards that method. Formal mandates have long since gone, and banks now set their own credit policies, but 1.33 survives as the rule of thumb that still shapes credit conversations.

body.title: What that means for Sunrise Ceramics in practice

children.text: Sunrise Ceramics has a working capital gap of ₹64 crore, that is current assets of ₹122 crore minus non-bank current liabilities of ₹58 crore.
Under the first method, the bank funds 75% of that gap, which is ₹48 crore. The company has drawn ₹35 crore of cash credit, so it sits comfortably inside that limit.

Under the second and stricter method, the permissible finance is 75% of total current assets minus non-bank current liabilities, that is ₹33.5 crore. Now the ₹35 crore already drawn exceeds the limit. This is the same story the current ratio of 1.21 tells: it is below 1.33, so by the older norms the company is running on more short-term bank money than its own contribution justifies. Chapter 6 works through both methods properly.

body.label: The benchmark most Indian credit officers still use
body.context: Traceable to the Tandon Committee, 1975, and reinforced by the Chore Committee, 1979. It is a convention, not a rule, and it means little without the industry context.

children.text: Four Ways These Ratios Mislead You
Liquidity ratios are snapshots of a single date, built from totals that hide their own quality. Here is where they break.

body.caption: The trap, and the question that defuses it

cells: A comfortable 1.21 that includes two-year-old receivables and unsold designs
What do the receivables and inventory ageing schedules show?
A ratio that improves every 31 March and sags through the year
What was the ratio at each quarter end, not just at year end?
A supermarket chain at 0.8 judged against a benchmark built for manufacturers
What is normal for this business model and this cash conversion cycle?
A high ratio read as strength
A ratio of 3.0 that comes from bloated stock and slow collections
Is this liquidity, or is it just cash trapped in the cycle?

children.text: The third trap deserves care, because it is the one that produces confidently wrong conclusions. A business that collects from customers before it pays suppliers can operate safely at a current ratio below 1. Hindustan Unilever ran a cash conversion cycle of about -89 days in FY2026, and Avenue Supermarts, which runs DMart, collected from shoppers in about a day while turning stock in roughly 37 days. Neither is in danger. Their models simply do not need a cushion of current assets, because cash arrives before the bills fall due.

body.title: The 30 March manoeuvre
body.prompt: On 30 March, Sunrise Ceramics uses ₹15 crore of a collection to pay down ₹15 crore of trade payables, purely so the year-end balance sheet looks better. Current assets fall to ₹107 crore and current liabilities to ₹86 crore. What is the new current ratio, to two decimal places?
body.explanation: The ratio improves from 1.21 to 1.24 without a single thing changing in the business. Paying down current liabilities with current assets always lifts a ratio that is already above 1. Note the reverse: for a company whose ratio is below 1, say ₹90 crore against ₹101 crore, the same ₹15 crore payment pushes the ratio down from 0.89 to 0.87.

body.text: This is why lenders ask for quarterly stock and book debt statements rather than trusting the March balance sheet. A ratio that is healthy on one date each year and weak on the other 364 is not a healthy ratio. It is a well-timed one.

columns.label: Genuine strength
points: Receivables are mostly under 60 days old
Inventory turns several times a year
Cash and bank balances are free, not pledged
The ratio is stable across all four quarters
The cash conversion cycle is stable or falling

columns.label: Trapped cash wearing a disguise
points: A large slice of receivables is over a year old
Inventory covers many months of sales
Bank balances are margin money against letters of credit
The ratio spikes only at year end
The cash conversion cycle keeps lengthening

children.text: One More Ratio Worth Knowing

Liquidity ratios ask whether the business can pay its bills. Working capital turnover asks a different and more useful question: how much revenue is the business generating from the money it has tied up?

body.caption: Rupees of sales generated per rupee of net working capital

children.text: Sunrise Ceramics turns its net working capital over 8.57 times a year. Higher is generally better, but only up to the point where the business is so thinly funded that one late payment stops production. And because net working capital sits in the denominator, this ratio becomes unstable as that number approaches zero and meaningless when it is negative, which is exactly the case for the FMCG and retail businesses discussed above. Use it within an industry, never across.

body.title: Name the ratio
body.textWithBlank: The ratio that removes inventory from current assets before dividing by current liabilities is called the ___ ratio.
body.explanation: The quick ratio, also called the acid test, measures whether short-term dues can be met without selling inventory. For Sunrise Ceramics it is 0.78 against a current ratio of 1.21.

body.title: Two suppliers, one credit decision
body.scenario: You handle vendor credit at a building materials distributor. Two suppliers want 60-day terms. Supplier A has a current ratio of 2.4 and a quick ratio of 0.7, with inventory covering about eight months of sales and receivables of which 28% are over a year old. Supplier B has a current ratio of 1.1 and a quick ratio of 0.95, collects in 22 days, turns inventory 11 times a year and has an unused cash credit limit of ₹12 crore.
body.prompt: Which supplier is the better credit risk, and what would you ask each of them for?
body.modelAnswer:
Supplier B, comfortably, despite the weaker headline current ratio.

Supplier A's 2.4 is built from inventory and stale receivables. Eight months of stock and more than a quarter of the book over a year old means much of that current asset pile will not become cash on any useful timetable. The quick ratio of 0.7 is the giveaway: strip the stock out and the cushion disappears.

Supplier B holds less cover on paper but the assets are live: 22-day collections, inventory turning 11 times a year, and a quick ratio close to 1. On top of that there is ₹12 crore of undrawn bank limit, which is real standby liquidity that no balance sheet ratio captures.

What to ask for: from A, the receivables and inventory ageing schedules, an explanation of the over-one-year book, and quarter-end ratios rather than the March figure. From B, confirmation of the undrawn limit from its banker and a look at the last four quarterly figures to check that the 22-day collection is normal and not a good quarter.

body.title: What does a falling current ratio tell you?
body.question: A manufacturer's current ratio has fallen from 1.45 to 1.21 over five years while sales have doubled. What is the most reasonable first conclusion?
options: The business is definitely in financial distress
Growth is being funded increasingly by short-term liabilities, which needs checking
The ratio has become more efficient and nothing needs checking
The company must have written off a large amount of inventory
body.explanation: A falling ratio alongside strong growth usually means current liabilities, typically bank borrowing and supplier credit, are growing faster than current assets. That can be deliberate and efficient, or it can be a slow slide into overtrading. The ratio flags the question; the ageing schedules and the cash conversion cycle answer it.

body.title: Sunrise Ceramics: current ratio and quick ratio over five years

children.text: One year of ratios tells you almost nothing. Five years of them tells you the direction of travel, and the direction here is unmistakable: both ratios have fallen every single year. That is the pattern worth acting on, long before any single year's number crosses a benchmark.

body.title: Sanity-check any liquidity ratio before you rely on it
steps: Recompute the ratio yourself from the balance sheet rather than accepting a quoted figure.
Compute the quick ratio alongside it, and treat a wide gap as a question about inventory quality.
Open the receivables and inventory ageing notes, and strip out what will clearly not convert to cash.
Check whether cash and bank balances are free or pledged as margin money.
Compare the ratio with the same company over four to five years, not with a textbook benchmark.
Compare with two or three companies in the same industry, never across industries.
Look at quarterly figures where available, to catch year-end window dressing.

children.text: Apply that checklist to Sunrise Ceramics and the picture sharpens. Remove the ₹11 crore of receivables over two years old, the ₹6 crore of dead inventory and the ₹4 crore of pledged margin money identified in Chapter 1, and current assets fall to ₹101 crore against current liabilities of ₹101 crore. The real current ratio is 1.00, not 1.21.

body.text: A liquidity ratio is a question, not an answer. It tells you where to look, and the ageing schedules tell you what you will find there.

body.label: Check a company's liquidity trend
body.description: Screener shows the balance sheet totals you need for a rough current ratio, plus the ratios section with debtor, inventory and payable days. Compare a retailer such as DMart with a manufacturer and watch how differently the same benchmark applies.

points: The current ratio, quick ratio and cash ratio ask progressively harsher versions of the same question, and should always be read together.
The 1.33 benchmark used across Indian banking traces back to the Tandon Committee of 1975, and is a convention rather than a rule.
A wide gap between the current and quick ratios means inventory is doing the heavy lifting, which is only reassuring if that inventory actually moves.
Paying current liabilities with current assets just before the year end lifts a current ratio above 1 without changing anything real.
Businesses with negative cash conversion cycles, such as FMCG companies and supermarkets, can operate safely below the usual benchmarks.
A high ratio can be trapped cash rather than strength, so always test it against the receivables and inventory ageing schedules.
Trends across four or five years, and across quarters, are far more informative than any single year's ratio.
